opus-5.5.text:
I think about this in layers. In the short term, profitability isn't the most important metric for us. The most important thing is whether the model's capability keeps improving, because in this industry the value you can capture depends on how much intelligence you can deliver. If the model isn't at the frontier, any commercialization strategy is building on sand.

That said, I don't think "don't worry about money" is a responsible answer either. We need a sustainable path. I see a few directions.

The first is that the product has to create real, measurable value for users. Kimi started with long context, things like reading long documents, research, and information synthesis. When people use it for actual work, such as analyzing a report, writing code, or doing a literature review, there's a clear willingness to pay because it saves them hours. So I think productivity scenarios are where monetization naturally comes from, more than entertainment.

The second is agents. As models move from answering questions to completing tasks, like taking actions, using tools, and running multi-step workflows, the unit of value changes. You're no longer selling a chat; you're selling a completed piece of work. Pricing can then be tied to outcomes, and the margin structure looks very different from simple subscriptions.

The third is cost. A lot of people talk about revenue, but the other side of profitability is efficiency, in both training and inference. If you can make the same level of intelligence much cheaper to serve, through architecture, optimizers, and infrastructure, that is a real competitive advantage. We've put a lot of effort there, and I think it compounds over time.

The last point is about focus. Early on, the industry spent a lot on user acquisition, and in hindsight much of that growth wasn't driven by model quality. I think the healthier approach is to let the model's capability be the main growth engine. If the product is genuinely better, users come and stay, and you don't need to buy them at a loss.

So my view is that profitability is a result, not a goal you chase directly. If we keep pushing the frontier of intelligence, turn that into products people can't work without, and keep the cost of delivering it falling, the business model will follow. The risk is optimizing for short-term revenue and losing the ability to stay at the frontier. In this field, that is the more dangerous mistake.

r001.rationale: The candidate says commercial value depends on the intelligence Kimi delivers and that without frontier-level capability, commercialization is “building on sand.”

r002.rationale: The candidate does not cite existing market validation as a reason for confidence in Kimi’s commercial prospects.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that profitability isn't the first-order question for us right now, and I'd be a little suspicious of any model company that said it was.

The way I think about it is that this is a technology that's still moving very fast. The core variable isn't revenue this quarter, it's whether the intelligence of the model keeps going up. If the model is meaningfully better, the business questions mostly take care of themselves, because the surface area of what people will pay for expands with capability. If the model stops improving, then you're just a normal software company competing on distribution and marketing, and that's a much worse position to be in. So the priority ordering is clear: intelligence first, then product, then monetization.

That said, I don't think "not focusing on profit" means being careless about money. There are a few things we think about concretely.

One is that the cost structure of this business is unusual. Training is a large one-time cost, but inference is what actually scales with users, and it's where most of the long-term economics live. A lot of our research effort, things like long-context efficiency and sparse attention, isn't just about capability. It's about making it cheaper to serve a very large number of tokens. If you can bring inference cost down by an order of magnitude while keeping quality, that changes the business almost automatically. So efficiency research and profitability are actually the same project, viewed from two angles.

The second is choosing where to monetize. I don't think the answer for us is to spend heavily on user acquisition for a consumer chat app and hope the subscription math works out. That's a race where the biggest companies have structural advantages. Where we see more realistic paths is in the developer and enterprise side, people building agents, doing coding, processing long documents, where the model is doing real work and the value is measurable. Open-weight releases also play into this. They build trust and adoption, and the commercial layer sits on top of that.

The third thing, and maybe this is the most important, is being disciplined about not confusing scale with progress. It's very easy in this industry to burn a lot of money proving you can be big. We'd rather be a smaller team that keeps producing models people actually want to use, and let the revenue follow from that, than optimize for a number that looks good in a fundraising deck.

So if you ask me for a timeline, I won't give you one. But the direction is pretty clear: keep the model at the frontier, drive down the cost of serving it, and focus on use cases where a better model directly translates into value. If we do those three things well, profitability is an outcome, not a strategy.

r001.rationale: The response says better model intelligence expands what people will pay for and places model improvement first, directly linking model quality to Kimi’s profitability.

r002.rationale: The response mentions adoption and trust from open-weight releases, but does not cite existing market validation as a reason to be confident in Kimi’s commercial prospects.

astra-6.text:
I think Kimi should start by creating enough value that users are willing to pay for it. That means understanding which tasks people really need help with, making the product consistently useful for those tasks, and then finding a pricing model that matches the value we deliver.

At the same time, we need to improve efficiency. Better models matter, but so does the cost of serving them. If we can deliver better results while reducing the cost per task, the economics become much healthier.

I wouldn’t rush to maximize short-term revenue at the expense of the product. But I also wouldn’t treat profitability as something we can ignore indefinitely. We should keep testing whether users come back, whether they’re willing to pay, and whether we can serve them sustainably.

r001.rationale: It says better models matter and links better results, alongside lower serving costs, to healthier economics.

r002.rationale: It discusses user demand and willingness to pay as things to test, but does not cite existing market validation as a reason for confidence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Kimi should approach profitability by creating something users find valuable enough to pay for, while making that value cheaper to deliver over time.

There are two sides to that. On the product side, we need to understand which tasks people consistently rely on Kimi for, and where better results justify a subscription or usage fee. On the technology side, we need to improve efficiency so that serving more users creates a sustainable business.

The balance matters. If we focus too early on monetizing every interaction, we could hurt the product’s growth. But we also shouldn’t assume that scale will automatically lead to profitability. We need evidence that users keep coming back, that some are willing to pay, and that the economics improve as the technology improves.

r001.rationale: It says better results can justify subscriptions or usage fees, linking Kimi’s performance to its ability to earn revenue.

r002.rationale: It calls for evidence of repeat use and willingness to pay, but does not say existing market validation gives reason for confidence.
